description: Question: in the network of who supervised whose doctorate, do a few advisors really collect most of the students, and is it a power law? Idea: heavy-tailed degree distributions and how to test a power law properly (Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009). Wikidata's doctoral-advisor relation (P184) links 334,857 students to 118,046 advisors (407,946 supervisions). Half the advisors have one recorded student, the mean is 3.46, yet 7 have 100 or more (C.-C. Jay Kuo 149): a geometric distribution with the same mean would expect 2×10⁻¹⁰ such advisors, and 0.006 with 50 or more where there are 194. The other direction, advisors per student, is thin-tailed (81% have one, at most 12) and an exponential beats a power law on it (likelihood-ratio z = −362). The method: plot the CCDF P(K ≥ k), not the histogram; estimate α by maximum likelihood, α = 1 + n / Σ ln(k/(x_min − ½)); choose x_min by the smallest KS distance; test against an alternative with Vuong's likelihood ratio. Aha: a straight line through the log-log histogram gives α = 2.79 (a line through the CCDF, 3.56), the MLE gives 1.71 from k = 1 and 4.04 ± 0.17 from the best x_min = 27, and α keeps rising with x_min: the curve bends, so the tail is heavy (cumulative advantage: the top 1% of advisors hold 11.6% of supervisions) but not a clean power law, and in the tail (1,158 advisors) a power law and an exponential can't be told apart (z = −0.65). Caveats: Wikidata records what editors entered (famous and recent academics, bulk imports from genealogy projects), so coverage, not only sociology, shapes the tail; the discrete fit uses the continuous ½-offset approximation; a lognormal or a power law with cutoff (not computed) may fit better; supervisions are counted over whole careers and centuries. Next: drill into one field (P101) or one era (the students' P569 birth dates); expand with the Mathematics Genealogy Project's own counts, or OpenAlex co-authorship degrees.
name: Power laws in the doctoral-advisor network
